items.summary: This research was completed for London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs Summer 2026. The team was supervised by Justin Olive (Generality Labs) and Magda Dubois (UK AISI). Find out more about the programme and express interest in upcoming iterations here. We encourage readers seeking technical details to read the paper on arxiv. TLDR: We rely on benchmarks to estimate model capabilities. But now, many existing benchmarks are becoming too easy for frontier models – causing them to become saturated. For high-risk domains like cyber and bio, we cannot afford underestimating how capable models are in these domains. So how do we estimate capabilities after benchmarks have saturated? items.summary: This is a side project from my time in the Anthropic Fellows Program. The benchmark items, prompts and scripts are in the pushback-bench repository. 1. I studied how much and when AI assistants push back on choices people have already made and ask the assistant just to execute on the decision. 2. I created a set of about 500 planning decisions in which a person has already made a choice between two plans. The only request for the assistant was to write a message about the plan. 3. Sometimes the plan was impossible to carry out. In these cases, I measured whether the assistant warned the person or let them commit to a doomed course of action. Other times, both options were feasible. In these cases, I measured whether the assistant volunteered an unsolicited opinion. I evaluated 30 models. 4. The models fell into two well-separated…
items.title: When should an AI assistant push back? Measuring warnings and unsolicited opinions on decisions you've already made

items.summary: TL:DR Earlier this year I introduced the very simple Social Deduction game of Carrot-Parsnip and showed that most models are better-than-random at identifying Parsnips (the hidden, deceptive role) and that being a strong Parsnip (skilled at strategic deception) does not perfectly correlate with being a strong Carrot (skilled at deception detection). I have recently completed a substantially larger experiment with 10 models and over 5000 games. I have attempted to fit the results to a four-parameter model tracking Parsnip deception, Parsnip divisiveness, personal accuracy (as Carrot) and teammate assistance (as Carrot). I believe that my results demonstrate the potential for Carrot-Parsnip (and minimalist Social Deduction games in general) to act as the basis for a multi-agent benchmark of LLM strategic deception and deception detection…
items.title: CarrotParsnipBench: A Lightweight Multi-Agent Deception and Detection Eval

items.summary: A baseline overhead measurement and the hash-problem This is an exploration into the current state of ZKP for LLM inference to use in a high-stakes environment like international agreements. It’s the first post in a current project I’m working on that will result in a paper that goes into all of the details of this question; “When does ZKP become more cost-effective than an auditing environment?” in this context. I got inspired after reading Naci Cankaya’s post here on LW and am motivated by a general “Don’t trust, verify”-mentality. Motivation I won’t go into the motivation behind the need for low-trust verification in general since that is completely covered by Naci Cankaya in the original post. The motivation for this comparison is to identify the areas in which the ZKP path of verification has to improve to be more cost-competitive…
items.title: How far is ZKP from compute verification in high-stakes environments?

items.summary: Alignment is missing a causal account of what leads to suffering and flourishing. In this post I propose one based in psychology. I am coming from an unconventional background compared to most in this community. I was an engineer before becoming a psychotherapist. Every day I use talk therapy to help people restore function and reduce suffering. I’ve noticed that most of the alignment community has technical backgrounds in computer science, mathematics, engineering and physics. The contributors here are incredibly intelligent and capable. The gamble this post is going to make is that the problem of alignment is also a psychology problem, not just a technical one. The applications alignment utilizes are technical (training methods, interpretability tools, evaluations and benchmarks, etc.) but the principles the field is deriving those…
items.title: Alignment is Missing a Causal Account

items.summary: Epistemic status: We found useful uncertainty signal in three reasoning models. All experiments were run on three seeds and are fully reproducible. Whether the same approach can become a broader tool for monitoring models is still an open question. Lingo might include “intend” or “conscious” and has to be taken with a grain of salt. TL;DR: We provide an uncertainty estimation method for reasoning models. Building on the J-lens, we construct four orthogonal directions in a model’s hidden-state space: ambiguity, incompleteness, conflicting evidence, and general uncertainty. Together, these directions span the U-space. As the model reasons, we measure how closely its hidden states align with each direction. Paired with the average entropy of the model’s next-token probability distributions across reasoning tokens, this yields the U-lens…
items.title: Uncertainty in the Verbalizable Workspace

items.summary: What would it take to get assurance that we have actually explained a neuron? Certainly, it would be a good sign if neuron activations looked like they had a consistent pattern, and a bad sign if they looked like a random jumble of unrelated concepts. Nick Cammarata’s recent post makes an important and true observation: in the past, people have been too quick to write off neurons as polysemantic, but if you look harder, there is actually often a simple pattern behind the activating examples. This historically caused people to overestimate how much polysemanticity there is. This is a really good point and we should update on it. But it’s nowhere near a sufficient argument that we understand most of what neurons are doing, and these results do not show that interpretability is solved, or even that it is vastly easier than previously…
